props.title: After the Fox
props.initialSlug: Master thief poses as director for ultimate heist

sections.content: After the Fox (1966) represents a fascinating intersection of European and American comedy, starring Peter Sellers at his chameleon-like peak. Written by Neil Simon and directed by Vittorio De Sica, this satirical heist film merges the sensibilities of Italian cinema with Hollywood farce. It follows master criminal Aldo "The Fox" Vanucci orchestrating an elaborate gold heist by posing as a filmmaker. The film cleverly predates other meta-commentaries on filmmaking like 8½ (1963) and Day for Night (1973), while incorporating elements of the popular heist genre seen in To Catch a Thief (1955) and The Pink Panther (1963).

sections.content: The film's satirical take on filmmaking and the emerging Italian cinema industry is particularly prescient. While Federico Fellini was exploring similar territory in 8½ (1963), After the Fox approaches it through a distinctly comedic lens. The movie anticipates later films about filmmaking like The Player (1992) and Living in Oblivion (1995), while maintaining the madcap energy of classic Peter Sellers vehicles like Dr. Strangelove (1964). SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Meta-Cinema Comedy

After the Fox established a template for self-referential film comedy that would influence later works like Bowfinger (1999) and Be Kind Rewind (2008). Its blend of crime caper and movie industry satire created a unique sub-genre that continues to resonate. The film's influence can be seen in everything from Get Shorty (1995) to Tropic Thunder (2008), where the mechanics of filmmaking become integral to the plot's criminal or comedic elements.
